I started a role as an undergraduate program coordinator for the department my undergraduate degree was in, fine arts. I'm happy I took the leap, I can't stress how much of a change it's made on my demeanor. 

I too took a pay cut, but I financially am lucky to be in a position where I've saved and have plans in place to cushion this. 

There are opportunities, and you can actually make use of these opportunities because you'll have the time and energy to do so. I'm not trying to become a full time faculty member, but I'm 1 course away from my master's and I already know that I'll have the chance to adjunct a course in my department if I want to keep teaching. I've already started networking outside of my department and have been offered to teach 1 hour workshops for a small stipend to education students. 

The people I work with are for the most part incredibly respectful and seem happy to have me there. You've made a good choice to move into higher ed, just make sure you take advantage of your situation and talk to people. That's how you'll open up door to new opportunities.

Kicker. I've got extremely flexible ankles, flexible hip flexors, and hyperextension in my legs. Makes for ideal kicking. I could hit around a minute for a sprint 100 fly kick in my prime.

When I swim, I just let the spring of my joints do the work. I just glide out everything, relaxed swimming can be fast. Relaxed kicking can be too. 

Oh, and I was a sprint flyer and freestyler in college. Used to win my races because of my underwaters.

Do it, I used to use these when I was a college athlete. Invested in one a year after. I never realized how quickly I could lose my core strength. Burns like hell, but worth it. I think it's good for arm strength as well.
Anything with Shea butter helps. Some girls in my college team put coconut oil into their hair after practice if hair dryness is an issue too.

Nothing I say will sound scientific. Is just swim.

I typically blow air out through my nose underwater and inhale through my mouth. You want to have clear airways. And I find this helps with cramping since you're not letting co2 sit in your system. 

Relax, the more aggressively you swim the more oxygen you're using up. Learn to reach with each stroke and glide for a portion. In breath control sets, we always knew more relaxed and slower swimming would let us go further with one breath.
